title: Elastic replica packing & topology swap — exploratory notes
content:
Purpose:
Quick working notes from an exploratory set of experiments probing how dynamic replica packing and on-the-fly interconnect/topology swaps affect per-request latency and throughput for pipelined+tensor-parallel LLM inference. Goal is to identify high-risk transitions and candidate mitigations (draining, backpressure shaping, NCCL policy knobs).

Background / why this felt important:
- We frequently autoscale and consolidate multiple customer replicas onto the same node to improve GPU utilization.
- Packing creates transient interconnect contention when new replicas spin up, migrate, or when PCIe/NVLink partitions change (maintenance, noisy neighbors).
- Most prior notes focus on steady-state throughput; this log looks at the transitions themselves (the spikes/microbursts that cause tail-latency regressions).

Hypotheses tested:
1) On-the-fly topology changes (e.g., moving a replica that changes NVLink connectivity group) cause short NCCL collective stalls that show up as 10–40 ms spikes on p99 despite steady p50.
2) Packing replicas that increase the number of simultaneous active PP/TP groups leads to sublinear throughput gains due to increased host staging and buffer thrash.
3) Introducing lightweight backpressure (token-leaky window at ingress) during topology swaps can reduce p99 by ~20–30% with <5% throughput impact.

Hardware / baseline software:
- Node type: 4xA100-40GB with NVLink mesh (pairwise), dual NIC RDMA (Mellanox CX6), PCIe Gen4 host.
- Cluster SW: Ubuntu 22.04, CUDA 12.1, cuDNN pinned, NCCL 2.18 with our modified NCCL policy hooks, custom runtime v0.78.
- Baseline model: 7B transformer, TP=2, PP=2 configuration (total 4 shards), KV cache enabled, context length 1024.
- Workload: synthetic arrival process: Poisson base (mean QPS 60), with bursts (sustained 200 qps for 10s every 60s) to emulate traffic spikes.

Experiment matrix (high level):
- Replica packing factor: {1 replica/node, 2 replicas/node, 3 replicas/node}
- Topology swap type: {none, in-node NVLink group change (simulate link flapping), cross-node migration}
- Ingress shaping: {no shaping, leaky-window=100ms, token-bucket=burst 50 -> sustained 25}
- NCCL policy: {default, aggressive-rendezvous, deferred-barrier}
- Each config: run 6 warmup cycles, 10 measurement cycles of 90s.

Instrumentation we relied on:
- Per-request token-level latency traces emitted from runtime (client -> token commit).
- NCCL logging at DEBUG with timestamps and collective ids (summarized).
- nvlink counters + per-GPU PCIe stall counters via nsys + custom BTL hooks.
- Host NIC RX/TX ring occupancy and kernel softirq latency sampling (100ms).

Key observations (short bullet list):
- Steady-state: packing 2 replicas/node increased aggregate throughput ~1.85x versus 1 replica, but p99 latency increased by ~15ms on average (tails grew).
- Transition spikes: when a topology swap occurred (simulated NVLink re-route on GPU 1), we saw synchronized NCCL collectives stall for ~30–55ms. These stalls aligned with host-to-gpu DMA bursts and NVLink arbitration spikes.
- Cross-node migration caused longer stalls (70–220ms) due to inflight host staging replays and RDMA queue rebuilds.
- Leaky-window ingress shaping (100ms) cut p99 spikes during swaps by ~28% with ~4% throughput drop (measured by stable-tail qps). This was the most effective low-effort mitigation.
- NCCL "deferred-barrier" policy reduced the amplitude of collective stalls by letting some pairwise communications complete without global synchronization; however, it increased average kernel completion jitter which pushed p50 up ~3–5ms for certain micro-batches.

Notable micro-observations:
- Host staging thrash: when number of active replicas > 2 on the node, host staging queues hit a saturation point leading to write-amplification on PCIe -> observable as repeating 1–2ms latency micro-jitters every 8–12 ms. These micro-jitters coalesced into p99 spikes under topology changes.
- RDMA queue rebuild: cross-node migration forces ephemeral recreate of RDMA qps; during the qpair rebuild window (~200–450 ms in our infra), requests either get queued in runtime or are retried and then cause double submission pressure leading to tail spikes.
- Kernel scheduling interplay: on some runs, higher replica packing led to more frequent kernel preemption on GPUs (context-switch flushes), visible as 0.5–3 ms GC-like pauses; these were rare but contributed to long tails when combined with comm stalls.

Representative numbers (TP=2,PP=2, 2 replicas/node, simulated NVLink swap):
- Aggregate throughput: 112 requests/sec (baseline 60 rps for 1 replica)
- p50 latency: 42 ms (baseline 38 ms)
- p95 latency: 118 ms (baseline 96 ms)
- p99 latency: 356 ms (spike windows, baseline 310 ms)
- Measured NCCL stall events: median 32 ms, 95th 68 ms during swap events

Example NCCL log snippet (timestamped simplified):
- 10:13:15.342 collective id=237 start allreduce size=64MB
- 10:13:15.375 collective id=237 wait barrier enter
- 10:13:15.410 collective id=237 stalled (nvlink arbitration backlog)
- 10:13:15.452 collective id=237 resume -> complete

Mitigation ideas tested and immediate notes:
1) Graceful drain window around topology mutation (recommended): set runtime to pause new arrivals for 150–300ms when a GPU link group is set to be migrated. Simple, effective; low engineering cost.
2) Token-leaky ingress shaping: we implemented as an optional per-node gate that spreads burst traffic across a 100ms window. Works well empirically; syncs with drain window for best effect.
3) NCCL policy tweaks (deferred barrier): reduces stall amplitude, but increases jitter and complicates correctness reasoning for some optimizer-launch ordering. Needs deeper validation in CI.
4) RDMA qpair fast-rebind: moved some qpair rebuild operations off hot path and re-used qpair contexts where possible; decreased cross-node migration stall median from ~210ms -> 130ms in our synthetic migration flows.
5) Replica placement heuristic: avoid packing replicas with overlapping peak-KV-cache footprint onto the same host; coarse estimate based on model size + expected context length. Reduced micro-thrash but costs utilization efficiency.

Open questions / risks:
- Do these patterns hold for larger PP (>=4) where pipeline bubble dynamics differ? Hypothesis: bubble amplification may make p99 worse under the same conditions. Need TP/PP sweep.
- Will real customer prompt distributions (long-tail of huge contexts) amplify the host-staging thrash more than our synthetic traces? Need to replay sampled production traces.
- Safety: deferred NCCL barrier interacts poorly with some kernel launch order assumptions in our runtime; we need a small formal proof-of-correctness for TENSOR+PIPE lined execution semantics under relaxed collectives.

Next steps / action items:
- [Priya] Run TP/PP sweep: TP in {2,4,8}, PP in {1,2,4} with packing factors 1..3 and report p50/p95/p99 + NCCL stall histogram. Due: 2024-09-20.
- [Asha] Wire up production trace replay using sampled requests for one low-volume customer; run migration-candidate scenarios. Due: 2024-09-27.
- [Diego] Prototype ingress leaky-window as config flag in runtime and run canary on dedicated capacity. Due: 2024-10-04.
- [Marcus] Draft a short proposal for "drain-on-topology-change" API and fence semantics. Due: 2024-09-12.

Misc notes / heuristics we captured:
- Conservative drain window suggestion: max(150ms, expected NCCL collective median*1.2).
- Use host NIC softirq sampling as a cheap early-warning signal for impending rebind pressure (softirq spikes precede RDMA qpair rebuilds by ~80–120ms in our runs).
- Prefer incremental placement changes (staggered migration) over simultaneous multi-gpu rebinds across a node: stagger gap ~200ms worked well.

Related links / references:
- internal PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/1487 (deferred-barrier experiment)
- confluence: perf/replica-packing-notes (work-in-progress)

Appendix: quick experiment checklist (for reproducibility)
1) Load nodes with baseline service, 2 replicas/node packing.
2) Start Poisson+burst generator, capture per-token traces.
3) Trigger topology swap script (simulate nvlink group change) on target GPU.
4) Capture NCCL debug logs + nsys perf counters.
5) Repeat 10x, keep full logs in s3://perf-archive/elastic-packing/ run-id XYZ.

End of notes.

(Informal/working doc: expect typos and incomplete analyses; intended to capture experimental intuition and immediate next steps.)
